newsitem.title: USA: Helms compares Canada-Cuba talks to appeasement.
newsitem.headline: Helms compares Canada-Cuba talks to appeasement.

text.p: Republican Senator Jesse Helms on Thursday compared the Canadian foreign minister's visit to Cuba this week to British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's appeasement of Adolf Hitler in 1938.

Helms, speaking after the swearing-in of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at the White House, was harshly critical of Canada but stopped short of recommending the United States take retaliatory action against it.

The remarks by Helms, chairman of the influential Senate Foreign Relations Committee, contrasted sharply with the views of President Bill Clinton, who said he was pleased Canada was trying to change Cuba's human rights policies but skeptical the overture would work.

Canada's foreign minister Lloyd Axworthy met with Cuban President Fidel Castro on Wednesday in Havana, with the two agreeing to work to advance their dialogue on a range of issues, including economic cooperation and human rights.
Asked what he thought of the visit, Helms, who chairs the influential Senate Foreign Relations Committee, replied: "Do you remember Neville Chamberlain? That's what Canada is."

"You had someone named Neville Chamberlain, he went over and sat down with Hitler and came back and said 'we can do business with this guy' and you saw what happened," he said. "One guy stood up and sad 'No no,' (and his) name was Winston Churchill."

"Now, if we're going to forget all principle and let Fidel Castro get by with all of his attrocities, then we better look at the status of our principles and Canada certainly should look at hers," he added.
Asked if the United States should consider retaliatory action against its northern neighbor, Helms replied. "Oh, I dont think we ought to get into that.

"They've been transhipping sugar from Cuba for a long time in violation of U.S. law," he added. "There's got to be some understanding of what a neighbor should be to another neighbor and they've been riding roughshod over us for long enough."
Helms is the co-author of a U.S. law that seeks to crack down on foreign companies that do business with Cuba.
Asked what he thought of the Canadian overture, Clinton took a markedly different tack.

"My reaction is I'm gratified that the Canadians, along with the Europeans, are now talking more to the Cubans about human rights and democratic reforms," Clinton told reporters after meeting United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan at the White House.

"I'm skeptical, frankly, that ... the recent discussions between the Canadians and the Cubans will lead to advances. I believe that our policy is the proper one, but I'm glad that the Canadians are trying to make something good happen in Cuba," he added.
At the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns echoed Clinton's skepticism but said the United States had "never questioned the wisdom of foreign minister Axworthy's trip."
"There's no reason that we can see that the tiger here is going to change its stripes," Burns told reporters.
